name: House of the Blackheads
label: House of Blackheads
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rātslaukums' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rātslaukums' (node/8649076355): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87495471: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'House of the Black Heads' (57 m across).
notes: Ornate rebuilt guild hall on Town Hall Square.

text.description:
The House of the Blackheads is one of the most eye-catching buildings in Riga's old town, with a gilded, richly decorated Dutch Renaissance façade that fills the frame from the square in front. It began in 1334 as a warehouse and meeting place for merchants, and from the mid-15th century it was used by the Brotherhood of Blackheads, a guild for unmarried merchants, shipowners and foreigners. The ornament you see today mostly dates from major works in the early 17th century. The building was wrecked in the fighting of June 1941, and the ruins were pulled down in 1948. It was rebuilt between 1996 and 2000, and more than 5,000 people paid to place a brick in the wall. It officially opened on 9 December 1999. The site is also linked with the first decorated Christmas tree, put up in 1510.

It photographs well because the façade is bright, detailed and sits right on an open square, so you can stand back and get the whole front in one shot. The best-known shot is a straight-on view from the middle of the square. For a wider postcard version, include the spire of St Peter's Church rising above the gable. Summer weekends are very crowded, and the Christmas market fills the square with stalls from late November to early January. Plan your shot around that, or accept a few people in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Riga, facing the open square of Rātslaukums, which is the usual place to photograph it from.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for Rātslaukums in Riga's old town; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for that square. From there the building is about 40 metres to the south, a short walk away, so you can see it clearly without walking right up to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square or the spire of St Peter's Church in the same shot. If the square is busy, a 2x telephoto setting lets you pick out the gilded details above the crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rātslaukums (Middle of the square, about 10 m south of the façade). A frontal view of the gilded Dutch Renaissance façade filling the frame, with the square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone upright and level so the sides of the building stay straight. Centre the gable on the middle line for a calm, symmetrical frontal shot. As an alternative from the same square, step back a little and use 0.5x or 1x to include the spire of St Peter's Church rising above the gable for the wider postcard view. Keep the phone level when you use ultra-wide, or the building will lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gilded part of the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the gold keeps its detail and does not wash out. Turn Live Photos on if you like, but it is a still subject, so a sharp single frame is the aim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, in the hour before sunset, when guides say the sun brings out the gilding. Summer weekends and the Christmas market period are the busiest.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed for free from the open square; the museum inside is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Riga Central Market
label: Central Market
camera_source: Commons cluster (16 photos). Moved 114 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 570 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/92054399: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Central Market' (553 m across).
notes: One of Europe's largest markets, in Zeppelin hangars.

text.description:
Riga Central Market is a huge food market housed in five long pavilions, and it is a good place for lively, colourful phone photos. The pavilions were built between 1924 and 1930 and reuse the metal frameworks of German Zeppelin hangars. Their hangar-derived roofs, with Neoclassical and Art Deco touches, give the buildings a shape you will not see at an ordinary market. Together with Old Riga, the market has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1998. It covers about 72,300 square metres and has more than 3,000 trade stands. It is described as Europe's largest market and bazaar.

The subject is big, so decide what you want before you start. From outside, the long rows of pavilions make a strong, repeating pattern. Inside and around the stalls, the photos are about people, piles of produce and signs. Keep a few shots wide to show the scale of the roofs, then move in for close pictures of stalls and colourful displays. Ask before photographing a stallholder close up, as a courtesy. Keep a hand on your bag, because the market is busy and petty theft is a known problem. Check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules about photography.
text.geographic_location: In Riga, on the bank of the Daugava, next to the railway and bus stations.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Walk south-east and the pavilions will come into view ahead of you. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the pavilion roofs and the long rows of buildings. Use the default lens (1x) for stalls and street scenes. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details on stalls from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Akmens tilts. The Old Town and modern left-bank buildings appear together in one frame, with the market, the railway bridge and the National Library visible across the river. Take your wide shots as you approach, then go in among the stalls for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the long pavilion roofs with a horizontal line so the buildings look straight. Stand at the end of a row of stalls so the lines lead the eye into the picture. Include a person walking past or a stallholder at work to show the scale. Then step in for a close shot of produce.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the stall and slide the exposure down a little so colours stay rich and bright areas do not wash out. Where the light is dim under a roof, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a pillar or your body. Portrait mode suits a single stall or a piece of produce.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go in the morning, when the stalls are likely to be busiest and fully stocked. Check the official site before you go for opening times.

text.access_note: The market is a working public market, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules inside the pavilions.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is about 9 minutes on foot from the middle of the market (567 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
Stalls are likely to be busiest and best stocked in the morning.
Light is dimmer under the pavilion roofs than outside.
It is polite to ask before photographing a stallholder close up.

name: Freedom Monument
label: Freedom Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Operas skvērs' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Operas skvērs' (way/1307456193): middle (178 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87182656: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Freedom Monument' (48 m across).
notes: Landmark symbol of Latvian independence.

text.description:
The Freedom Monument honours soldiers killed in the Latvian War of Independence (1918–1920) and is a national symbol of Latvian freedom. It was unveiled in 1935 and stands 42 metres tall, built of granite, travertine and copper. At the top, a 9-metre copper figure of Liberty holds up three gilded stars, one each for Vidzeme, Latgale and Courland. Locals call her Milda. The money for the monument came from private donations. It also has a place in more recent history: on 14 June 1987 about 5,000 people gathered here to lay flowers, a moment that helped renew the independence movement.

It photographs well because the slim column rises clear of everything around it, so even a phone shot has a strong, simple shape. Seen from Opera Square, the monument stands across the canal, with the canal-side plantings in the foreground and the water adding depth. Around the base are sculpture groups showing Latvian history and culture, which are worth a closer look once you walk over. If you want a different angle, the lime-tree avenue of Brīvības bulvāris gives a view framed by trees, and Bastejkalna Park gives lawns and flowerbeds in front, or a wider view from higher ground.

The guard changes on the hour during the day and people gather then, so allow for crowds. Keep a respectful distance from the guards and your voice down.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands in the centre of Riga on Brīvības bulvāris (Freedom Boulevard), next to the Old Town. The nearby section of the street is pedestrianised and includes a bridge over the city canal.
text.directions_text: The monument is to the north of this spot, about 140 m away, a short walk if you want to go across for a closer look. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the monument, the canal and the plantings together. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the figure of Liberty and the top of the column.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Operas skvērs (Opera Square, across the canal from the monument). The monument seen across the water with the flowering canal-side plantings in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the column on a vertical line, with the plantings and water filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the column does not lean. For a different view, try the lime-tree avenue of Brīvības bulvāris, or Bastejkalna Park for lawns and flowerbeds in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the monument to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone and sky keep their detail. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, as it makes the monument look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or evening is usually calmer. The guard changes on the hour in the daytime, so expect more people then. The midday sun is generally from the south, behind you when facing north.

text.access_note: The monument is in an open public space, free to visit and open at all hours.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or evening is usually quieter than the middle of the day.
The midday sun is generally from the south, behind the photographer when facing north.
The canal-side plantings are in flower only in some seasons.
From about 140 metres away, a phone's 2x or higher zoom is enough to show the figure of Liberty at the top.

name: Riga Cathedral
label: Riga Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Doma laukums' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Doma laukums' (node/8649076357): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45105364: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Riga Cathedral' (103 m across).
notes: The largest medieval church in the Baltics, on Dome Square.

text.description:
Riga Cathedral is the big brick church that dominates the Old Town skyline, and it is the landmark most visitors want a picture of. Its formal name is the Cathedral Church of Saint Mary, and it is the Evangelical Lutheran cathedral of Latvia's capital. Bishop Albert founded it in 1211, and it is considered the largest medieval church in the Baltic states. It has undergone many modifications over its history. It also has a weathercock, like the other old churches in the city. Recent work has kept it looking sharp: the copper roof over the nave was replaced in 2011 and the tower was re-plated in 2015.

It photographs well because the square gives you room to step back and fit the brick walls and tower into one frame. Cafés and people at the base add scale and life. If you want a different view, try the narrow cobbled Krāmu iela, where the cathedral closes the end of the street, or look down on the tower from Svētā Pētera baznīca (check the official site before you go). Early morning gives the emptiest square, and the late afternoon light is softer. In December the Christmas market in the square can block views and crowd the space.
text.geographic_location: Riga Cathedral stands in the Old Town of Riga, not far from the River Daugava, on the square called Doma laukums.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head for the Old Town and Doma laukums. Once you are in the square, the tower is easy to spot and hard to miss. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade and tower. If the square is crowded and you cannot step back far enough, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the tower top, the weathercock and brickwork details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Doma laukums (in front of the cathedral's west facade). The full brick facade and tower of the cathedral filling the frame, with the cafés and street life of the square around its base.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower on a vertical line so the walls do not lean. Leave a little space above the tower and some foreground at the bottom, such as café tables or people. For an alternative, Krāmu iela gives a narrow cobbled-street view with the cathedral at the end.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus and drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. On a quiet morning, try a Live Photo to catch people crossing the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 8 am for an almost empty square, or after 4 pm when the light softens. The square is busiest from about 10 am to 3 pm.

text.access_note: Doma laukums is a free, open public square, but for going inside the cathedral (a working church) check the official site before you go.

name: Swedish Gate
label: Swedish Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Zviedru vārti' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4220818289: the OpenStreetMap point 'Swedish Gate'.
notes: The only surviving gate in the old city wall.

text.description: The Swedish Gate (Zviedru vārti) is a short brick archway set into the old Riga city wall, on Torņa iela. It was built in 1698 as part of the wall, to give access to barracks outside the city, and it is the only one left of the town's former eight gates. That alone makes it worth a stop, and it is also a neat subject for a phone camera. The passage works like a frame: brick walls close in on both sides, and the street beyond shows up as a bright rectangle at the far end. That contrast of dark tunnel and daylight gives a simple photo real depth. There is a well-known local legend too, about a girl who met a Swedish soldier here in secret, which makes a good caption. The gate is small, so it is quick to photograph, and a few minutes is plenty. Tour groups often pass through and can block the view, so a little patience helps. If you want a different angle, try the Torņa iela side, where the archway sits beside the long yellow Jēkaba kazarmas building, or Trokšņu iela, where you can show the gate with the cobbled street running along the city wall. Guides suggest going early in the morning for an emptier street.
text.geographic_location: In Riga's Old Town, set into the surviving stretch of the old city wall at Torņa iela 11, next to the long yellow Jēkaba kazarmas building.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town and head to Torņa iela, where the gate stands at number 11. Once you are on Torņa iela, the gate is easy to spot in the wall. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straight view through the arch. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include the full curve of the brick and the street ahead, but keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look through the passage toward the street, so the brick framed from inside, with light and shadow along the tunnel-like arch, fills the picture. If the passage is closed, shoot from just outside the archway looking in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the middle of the arch on the centre line so both walls look balanced. Let the bright street at the far end be the focus of the shot. For a second picture, step out to Torņa iela and photograph the archway beside the yellow Jēkaba kazarmas building, or use Trokšņu iela to show the gate with the cobbled street beside the city wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright end of the passage to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the street is not washed out. If the brick looks too dark, try a slightly higher setting and compare the two shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when there are fewer tour groups and the street is likely to be emptier.

text.access_note: The gate may be open at all hours, or you may only be able to photograph it from outside, so check on the day, and be ready to photograph from outside.

name: National Library of Latvia
label: National Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'National Library of Latvia' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1133733: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Modern glass building across the Daugava, with a view of the old town.

text.description:
The National Library of Latvia is the building known as the Castle of Light (Gaismas pils). It was designed in 1989 by the Latvian-American architect Gunnar Birkerts and opened in 2014, on the left bank of the Daugava, away from the Old Town. The institution itself is much older: it was founded in 1919 as the State Library, and today it holds more than 5 million titles.

For phone photographers it works in two ways. From outside, the large glass-and-stone shape stands out against the sky. Inside, the upper floors give a wide view over the Old Town roofs, the Stone Bridge and the river, and the tiered book shelving makes a strong interior picture with plenty of lines and layers.

The upper-floor glass is tinted or dotted, which can spoil shots. The Level 3 seating area is a better choice than the very top floor for clearer pictures. Take a few frames of the shelves, then walk to a window for the skyline. If you want the building itself in the frame, the Stone Bridge (Akmens tilts) shows the library across the river, sometimes with the railway bridge beside it. Another option is the tower of St. Peter's Church, which looks back across the river toward the library.
text.geographic_location: The library stands on the left bank of the Daugava, across the river from Riga's Old Town.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop was found for this spot. The library stands on the left bank of the Daugava, across the river from the Old Town. Once you arrive, go inside and head up to the Level 3 seating area. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the tiered shelving and the big interior spaces. Use the default lens (1x) for the window views over the river and Old Town. A 2x-3x zoom, if your phone has one, picks out single rooftops and spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Choose the Level 3 seating area rather than the very top floor. From there the photo shows the Old Town, the Stone Bridge and the Daugava through the windows, with the tiered book shelving nearby for interior shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the river or the bridge up with a horizontal grid line. For the interior, stand back and let the tiered shelves lead the eye into the frame. If you want the library from outside, the Stone Bridge (Akmens tilts) gives a view of the building across the Daugava.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Hold the phone close to the glass, with your hand shading the lens, to cut reflections and the dotted pattern. Tap the Old Town on screen to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit during the library's opening hours, ideally on a clear day when the Old Town skyline is sharp. Check the official site for the times, as they vary.

text.access_note: The library is a public building where reaching the upper floors is reported to be free with a visitor pass, but opening hours vary, the view can close for private events and the outdoor roof deck is reportedly guided-tour only, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The library faces the Old Town across the river.
Holding the phone close to the glass and shading it reduces reflections.
A clear day gives sharper views of the Old Town skyline.
From outside, the building stands out against the sky.

name: Museum of the Occupation of Latvia
label: Occupation Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Latviešu strēlnieku laukums' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Latviešu strēlnieku laukums' (node/8649076356): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1586390: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Black modernist building on Latvian Riflemen Square.

text.description:
The Museum of the Occupation of Latvia is a black, boxy modernist building that stands out from the pale stone and spires of the Old Town nearby. The best-known view is across Latviešu strēlnieku laukums, with the tall granite Riflemen Monument in the foreground, the museum's dark block behind it, and St Peter's spire and the House of the Blackheads peeking in at the side. That puts the monument, the museum and the Old Town skyline in a single frame.

The building dates from 1971, when the Soviets put it up to mark what would have been Lenin's 100th birthday. Until 1991 it served as a museum to the Red Latvian Riflemen. The present museum was founded in 1993 and tells the story of Latvia's occupations between 1940 and 1991. After a long renovation, the new permanent exhibition opened on 1 June 2022. A wall-shaped memorial called the Tactile of History was unveiled beside the building in 2021. The Riflemen Monument is a Soviet-era memorial and is still debated in Latvia, so it is worth knowing a little of the story when you photograph it.

Older photos online may show the museum in a different building on Raiņa bulvāris 7, where it was housed during the works. For your own picture, keep the monument large and low in the frame, and let the dark façade sit behind it. There is also a tighter, quieter version of the shot from the monument end of the square.
text.geographic_location: In central Riga, on Latviešu strēlnieku laukums, the museum's own square. St Peter's spire and the House of the Blackheads can be seen from here.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town and head for Latviešu strēlnieku laukums (the museum's address is number 1). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view, then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the square and the sky. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the tighter frame of the monument with the museum behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Latviešu strēlnieku laukums (across the square from the museum, with the Riflemen Monument in the foreground). The museum's black modernist block behind the granite Riflemen Monument, with St Peter's spire and the House of the Blackheads visible to the side. The subject is to the north-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the monument on one of the vertical lines, with the museum filling the other part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the building's straight edges stay straight. For a quieter alternative, walk to the monument end of the square and shoot the monument with the museum rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum's dark façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the black walls keep some detail. If the sky is very bright, the HDR setting in your camera app can help.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight when the sky is bright but not harsh works well for the dark façade. Early in the day the square is usually quieter, which makes it easier to keep people out of the foreground.

text.access_note: The square is open public space; for the museum's interior, opening times and any exterior access, check the official site before you go.

sources.title: Museum of the Occupation of Latvia

name: Riga Castle
label: Riga Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pils laukums' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Pils laukums' (node/12290889293): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1393926: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Riga Castle' (174 m across).
notes: Residence of the President of Latvia, on the Daugava bank.

text.description:
Riga Castle is a long, pale building on the bank of the Daugava, and it photographs best from the open square in front of it. For the whole facade, step back onto Pils laukums, which gives you clear space to take it all in.

The castle was founded in 1330 and rebuilt between 1497 and 1515, after Rigans destroyed it in 1484. When it was rebuilt, two of the original four square corner towers were replaced by round ones, so look for that mix of shapes. The Swedes added large annexes in 1641, and the building kept being extended until the 19th century. Today the northern part is the official residence of the President of Latvia, and the southern part holds several museums.

The castle was damaged by a serious fire in June 2013, during restoration work that began in December 2012. Take a moment to notice the roofline and upper floors, as they are part of what you are photographing.

For a phone, the main job is fitting the width of the building into the frame. Start with the whole facade, then move in for details such as the towers and windows. If you have time, two other views are worth a look: the bridge called Vanšu tilts for the castle reflected in the river, and Bastejkalns for a view from above.
text.geographic_location: Riga Castle stands on the bank of the Daugava river in Riga, between Stone Bridge and Vanšu Bridge, facing the open square Pils laukums (Castle Square).
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Daugava riverbank in central Riga, by taxi or hired scooter, and ask for Pils laukums (Castle Square). The castle is on the embankment between Stone Bridge and Vanšu Bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit as much of the front of the castle in as you can. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look if you can step further back onto Pils laukums. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the round towers, roofline and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pils laukums. The full front facade of the castle, framed from the open square directly in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building up with a horizontal line, holding the phone level so the facade does not lean. Leave a little sky above the roof and some open square below. For a different view, try Vanšu tilts for the castle reflected in the Daugava with the old town skyline, or Bastejkalns for a view from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale walls keep their detail. Take a few shots at different zoom levels so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and golden.

text.access_note: The square in front of the castle is open to walk onto, but the northern part is the President's residence and the museums are in the southern part, so check the official site before you go for any visits or restrictions.

name: Albert Street
label: Albert Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alberta iela 4' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Alberta iela' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/15666239: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Alberta iela' (260 m across).
notes: The main street for Riga Art Nouveau architecture.

text.description: Albert Street (Alberta iela) is a short street in central Riga lined with Art Nouveau apartment buildings, and it is a good place to point a phone upwards. The street was built in 1901 and named after Bishop Albert, who founded Riga in 1201. Many of the buildings were designed by Mikhail Eisenstein, whose decorative, unusual facades are the reason people come. Other architects, including Konstantīns Pēkšēns and his pupil Eižens Laube, worked on the street at the same time, so the facades vary from door to door. The most photographed one is Alberta iela 4, where a carved three-faced head relief sits above the entrance arch. A little further along, number 13 has dense relief work, a peaked top and grotesque masks. Number 12 was Pēkšēns' own home and has housed the Riga Art Nouveau Museum since April 2009. The street is photogenic because every building competes for attention, with faces, patterns and curved ornament at every level. Look for two kinds of picture: a wide shot with several facades side by side, and a close shot of one carved detail. This is a residential street, so keep voices down, stay on the pavement and do not block doorways. Mornings before 09:00 are quietest. Weekends and the middle of the day are busier with tour groups.
text.geographic_location: Albert Street is in central Riga, a short street of Art Nouveau apartment buildings. Several university and college buildings, and a couple of embassies, are on or next to it.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for central Riga and walk to Alberta iela. The middle of the street is to the south-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the head-on view of the entrance facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of a building or several facades along the street. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved faces and masks.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Alberta iela 4 (front facade above the entrance arch). The entrance facade with its carved three-faced head relief, seen head-on from the pavement across the street. The middle of Albert Street lies to the south-east of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the entrance arch and keep the carved head in the upper half of the frame. Then take a wider shot of the street, with several ornate facades side by side and the corner where the two streets meet. For another view, walk along to Alberta iela 13 and frame its relief-covered facade, peaked top and masks with the street in front. Stay on the pavement.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines so the vertical edges of the buildings stay straight when you tilt the phone upwards. Tap on the carved stonework to focus, and nudge the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out the top of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings before 09:00, when tour groups are absent and the north-facing facades get good light in summer. Avoid weekends and the hours from 11:00 to 15:00, when groups crowd the street.

text.access_note: Albert Street is an open public street, but it is residential, so be considerate of residents; if you plan to visit the Riga Art Nouveau Museum at number 12, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: A narrow street with tall facades means the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is useful for fitting a whole building in.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean, so gridlines help keep them straight.
A bright sky can wash out the top of a facade, so lowering the exposure slider can help.

name: Cat House
label: Cat House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tirgoņu iela' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Tirgoņu iela nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1307300: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cat House' (54 m across).
notes: Art Nouveau building with the black cats on the roof.

text.description:
The Cat House (Kaķu nams) is a yellow corner building at 10 Meistaru iela in Riga's old town. Friedrich Scheffel designed it and it was built in 1909, in a medieval style with some Art Nouveau touches. Its fame comes from the two cat sculptures on the roof turrets, each with an arched back and a raised tail. The best-known legend says the owner was refused membership of the Great Guild, whose house stands across the street. In revenge he had the cats placed with their tails towards the guildhouse. In the story the cats were later turned round to face it. There is an older version too, in which the quarrel was with the city council and the Town Hall.

It photographs well because the story is visible in the picture. From there the cats appear to look down at the Guild hall, and one frame tells the whole tale. It is also a quieter spot than the close view at the corner. For a closer look at the turrets, try Meistaru iela and shoot upwards. The building is private, so photograph it from the street.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Riga, at 10 Meistaru iela, close to and across the street from the Great Guild.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Meistaru iela in Riga's old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the wide shot that includes both the Cat House and the Great Guild. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit both. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the cats on the turrets closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Tirgoņu iela (stepped back from the corner toward the Great Guild, across the street). The Cat House and the Great Guild in a single frame, with the cats appearing to look down at the Guild hall. The Cat House lies to the north-east of here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the facade does not lean. Put the cats on a top third line and leave the Guild building on the other side of the frame. For a different view, walk to Meistaru iela and look up at the two cats on the corner turrets of the yellow facade. The second cat sits on a smaller gable pavilion and is hard to see from the corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the yellow keeps its colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer on the street. Pick whatever time the sun is not straight behind the cats.

text.access_note: The building is private and only the ground-floor restaurant is open to the public, so photograph it from the street.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon is usually calmer on the street.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps stop a bright sky washing out the facade.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit both buildings into the frame on a narrow street.

name: Three Brothers
label: Three Brothers
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mazā Pils iela' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Mazā Pils iela nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/348059067: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Three Brothers' (31 m across).
notes: The oldest group of medieval houses in Riga, on Mazā Pils iela.

text.description:
The Three Brothers are three old houses standing shoulder to shoulder on Mazā Pils iela in Riga's Old Town. Together they make up the oldest group of dwelling houses in the city, and each one shows a different stage in how homes were built. No. 17 is the oldest, from the late 15th century, with stepped gables and Gothic touches. No. 19 has an exterior from 1646, with a stone doorway added in 1746. No. 21 is a narrow Baroque house that probably took its present look in the late 17th century. Today the group holds the Latvian Museum of Architecture, and it received the European Heritage Label in 2020.

It photographs well because the three facades differ in height, colour, window pattern and roofline, yet they sit in one tidy row. The standard picture is from the opposite side of the lane, where all three fit in one frame and the cobbles make a clean foreground. In the early morning the facades catch the sun and the lane is quiet, so you can shoot without tour groups walking through the picture. For a second angle, move along the lane to include the cathedral spire rising behind the rooftops. Keep your phone upright and level so the gables don't lean, and give yourself a little space around the edges for cropping later.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Vecrīga (Riga's Old Town), on Mazā Pils iela, very close to Dome Square and the Saeima building.
text.directions_text: Make your way into the Old Town and to Dome Square, then follow the signs or your map to Mazā Pils iela; the houses are at Nos. 17, 19 and 21, close to the square. Look for the three differently shaped facades side by side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the whole row from across the lane. If you can't step back far enough, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use a 2x telephoto lens, if your phone has one, for a close-up of the gables or the stone doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mazā Pils iela (opposite side of the lane, about 10 m south of No. 17). All three houses (Nos. 17, 19 and 21) in a single row, with the facades lit by morning sun. From here Nos. 17, 19 and 21 all fit in one frame, with the cobbles as a foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the houses up with the horizontal lines so the row sits level. Keep the phone upright and don't tilt it upwards, or the facades will lean. For an alternative, walk a little along the same lane to catch the cathedral spire rising above the rooftops behind the row.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sunlit walls don't wash out. Take a few shots in a row in case someone walks through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, roughly 7:00 to 10:00, when the facades face the sun and the lane is quiet.

text.access_note: The facades can be photographed from the public lane; the rear courtyard is reached through the Latvian Museum of Architecture, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps when you cannot step back far enough in a narrow lane.
Tilting a phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps stop sunlit walls from washing out.

name: Latvian Academy of Sciences
label: Academy of Sciences
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1615464: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Soviet-era skyscraper with an observation deck.

text.description:
Rising 108 metres above the Latgale suburb, the Latvian Academy of Sciences is one of the most recognisable shapes on Riga's skyline. Locals call it "Stalin's birthday cake" or "the Kremlin", and it is easy to see why: the stepped, tiered tower and tall central spire follow the style of Stalin-era skyscrapers elsewhere in the Soviet Union. It was built between 1951 and 1961 and was the first skyscraper in Latvia. The walls carry hammer-and-sickle symbols alongside Latvian folk ornaments, which makes for interesting close-up photos. The star that once topped the spire was removed after Latvia regained independence in 1991.

It photographs well because the tower is so tall and symmetrical, with strong vertical lines and plenty of surface detail. From the phone icon on the map you are right at the building, so the big question is how to fit it in. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the whole tower, and switch to the default lens (1x) or the zoom for the carved ornaments and the upper tiers. A 17th-floor balcony, 65 metres up, is open for public viewing and gives a view over the city, so it is worth a second set of photos if you have time. Opening arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Academy stands in Riga's Latgale suburb. It is a very tall building that dominates the area around it.
text.directions_text: No Riga tram or rail stop is listed close to this spot, so start from the Latgale suburb, or from the city centre, and come by taxi or hired scooter. The tower is tall enough to spot from a distance, so you can use it as a guide as you approach. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to get the whole tower into the frame. Then use the default lens (1x) for the main body, and the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire, the carved ornaments and the hammer-and-sickle details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are very close, so hold the phone upright and tilt it slightly upwards to take in the height of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower's edges with the vertical lines, so the sides don't lean inwards. Keep the spire centred for a symmetrical shot, or step to one side and place the tower on a third for a more dynamic one. For detail shots, zoom in on the ornaments and reliefs rather than trying to cram everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so a bright sky doesn't wash out the stonework. If the sky is a flat grey, tap on the building and keep the sky to a thin strip.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A clear day with good daylight shows off the stonework and the carvings. At dusk, when the lights come on, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The building can be photographed from outside, but the 17th-floor viewing balcony is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go.

name: St. Peter's Church
label: St. Peter's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Skārņu iela' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Skārņu iela nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45069779: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. Peter's Church' (98 m across).
notes: Gothic church whose tower has a viewing platform.

text.description: St. Peter's Church is a Lutheran church in Riga's old town, and its tall, slim spire is one of the most recognisable shapes on the city skyline. The church is first mentioned in 1209, and the tower you see today has a long history of fires and rebuilding. Artillery fire destroyed the church in 1941. Restoration work began in 1954, and the main works ran from 1967 to 1983, with the interior finished in 1984. A gilded rooster sits on top of the steeple, and the clock has only an hour hand. The view looks along the church's front. The spire rises above the old-town buildings and sits beside the modern apartment block at Skārņu iela 11. The pairing of a medieval tower with a modern building makes a more interesting picture than a straight shot of the church. It also works well after dark, when the street is lit. If you want a quieter close-up, walk round to the Bremen Town Musicians statue, where the bronze figures stand against the curved stonework at the back of the church. The church is a working parish church with a tower viewing deck, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
text.geographic_location: In the old town of Riga, on Skārņu iela, the street where St. Peter's Church has its main entrance.
text.directions_text: Make for Riga's old town and look for Skārņu iela. Once you are on Skārņu iela, the church is to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The spire is easy to spot above the rooftops, so keep looking up as you walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the whole spire and the apartment block fit into the frame from the street. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the steeple and the rooster.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Skārņu iela (street-level view along the church's front, where the apartment block at Skārņu iela 11 frames the spire). The church's tall spire rising above the old-town street, paired with the modern apartment building at Skārņu iela 11, as in a night composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line, so the tower does not look as if it leans. Let the street and the modern apartment building take up one side of the frame, and the spire rise above it. For a quieter alternative, take a close-up of the Bremen Town Musicians statue with the curved back wall of the church behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest part of the spire to focus and lower the exposure slider a little, so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk or evening, when the street lights are on, suits the street-and-spire composition. The street can be photographed at any time of day.

text.access_note: The street is an open public street, but the church and its tower viewing deck may have their own visiting rules and tickets, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The street is fairly narrow, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is likely to be needed to fit the whole spire in.
Dusk or evening, when the street lights are on, suits this view.

name: Powder Tower
label: Powder Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vaļņu iela' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Vaļņu iela nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45018613: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Powder Tower' (21 m across).
notes: Medieval round tower, the last of the old city's defences.

text.description: The Powder Tower is a chunky round tower of dark red brick that stands in Riga's Old Town, once part of the town's defences. It photographs well because it is simple and solid: one strong shape, with old walls and a street leading the eye towards it. The tower was first mentioned in 1330 as the Sand Tower. The version you see now was built in 1650 on the surviving basement of an earlier tower that had been destroyed. It gets its name from the 17th century, when gunpowder was apparently stored inside. Later it served as a prison, and weapons were kept there until 1883. Between 1937 and 1940 it was renovated and became part of the Latvian War Museum. Look closely at the walls and you can spot cannonballs set into the brickwork, placed there to commemorate the Second Northern War. For the classic photo, stand at the north-western end of Vaļņu iela and face the tower. From there it fills the view at the end of the street, and the Old Town street leads towards it. If you want a different view, try Torņa iela, where Jacob's Barracks sits in the same frame as the tower. For a close detail shot of the brickwork and cannonballs, go up to the tower itself. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the tower's sides stay upright.
text.geographic_location: At the north-western end of Vaļņu iela in Riga's Old Town, near Torņa iela and Jacob's Barracks.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from the Old Town and walk towards its north-western edge. Head for the round red-brick tower and look for the north-western end of Vaļņu iela. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand, which shows the whole tower with the street leading to it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the tower will not fit, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the brickwork and cannonballs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vaļņu iela (north-western end of the street, facing the tower). The red-brick round tower filling the view at the end of the street, with the Old Town street leading toward it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower slightly off-centre, letting the street run into the bottom of the frame. Keep the phone upright to avoid leaning walls. For a variation, try Torņa iela, where the tower and Jacob's Barracks fit in the same frame, or move close to the tower for the cannonballs set in the brick.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the red brick keeps its colour. Wipe your lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the street is quieter, such as early in the day, so you can get the tower without people crossing the frame. Soft light suits the red brick.

text.access_note: The streets around the tower are open public space; if you want to go inside the Latvian War Museum, check the official site before you go for opening days.

name: Bastejkalns Park
label: Bastion Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bastejkalns' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bastejkalns' (node/520014852): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1419373599: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bastejkalna parks' (306 m across).
notes: Hilltop park along the city canal.

text.description: Bastejkalns Park is a spacious green park on the northern edge of Riga's Old Town, laid out around a small hill, the Bastion Hill, and a quiet stretch of the city canal. It sits where the city's fortress ramparts once stood. They were pulled down in 1856, and the grounds were then reshaped into gardens and paths, with the landscape architect Georg Kuphaldt a key figure in the planting. A dolomite waterfall cascade from 1898 still survives, and the park now also holds the Freedom Monument and several other monuments. It photographs well because it gives you layers: water, trees, bridges and, from the top of the hill, a view over the canal and treetops toward the Freedom Monument and the Old Town skyline. The park also has a good mix of trees and shrubs, including magnolias and forsythia that flower in spring, which adds colour to your pictures. For a phone, the best plan is to climb the hill first for the wide view, then wander down to the canal for closer pictures of water, railings and bridges. If you only have time for one shot, make it the view from the hilltop. Keep your phone's gridlines on to hold the horizon level, and take a few frames as you walk, because the view changes with each step. For a second angle, the Love Bridge gives a close view of the canal and its padlock-covered railings, framed by trees and the park paths.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town district of Riga, on the northern edge of the Old Town, beside the city canal and close to the Freedom Monument.
text.directions_text: Start from the Old Town and head for its northern edge, where the park and the canal begin. If you are coming from further out, use a map app and search for Bastejkalns. Once in the park, follow the paths up the small hill in the middle. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view from the hill, as it shows the canal, trees and skyline in a natural way. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the park's greenery in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the Freedom Monument or the Old Town rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bastejkalns (top of the Bastion Hill, the small hill in the middle of the park). A view down over the canal and the park's greenery toward the Freedom Monument and the Old Town skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line so the canal and trees fill the lower part of the picture. Use a branch or the edge of a path as a frame at the side. Then zoom in for a second shot of the Freedom Monument. For a closer alternative, walk down to the Love Bridge for the canal, its railings and the park paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the monument to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Wipe your lens before you start, as park air and pockets leave marks.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the greenery and the skyline than harsh midday sun. Spring flowers and autumn leaves add colour, but check the hill paths first if the ground is wet or icy.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space, but check the official site before you go for the current state of the canal and hill paths.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the greenery and skyline better than harsh midday sun.
Hill paths may be wet or icy in poor weather.
Trees in full leaf may partly screen the view from the hilltop in summer.

name: Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ
label: Nativity Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanade' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Esplanāde' (way/727332005): middle (556 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/87872119: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kristus Piedzimšanas pareizticīgo katedrāle' (73 m across).
notes: Neo-Byzantine Orthodox cathedral with golden domes.

text.description:
The Cathedral of the Nativity of Christ is the largest Orthodox cathedral in the Baltic provinces, built in a Neo-Byzantine style between 1876 and 1883 to a design by Nikolai Chagin and Robert Pflug. It was a Russian Empire project, and in the early 1960s the Soviet authorities closed it and turned it into a planetarium. Since Latvia regained independence in 1991 it has been restored, and in 2010 the bell tower and dome were gilded.

It photographs well because it is big, richly decorated and has plenty of space around it. From the Esplanade, the park in central Riga where the cathedral can be seen, the building stands large and unobstructed across open green lawn. That gives you a clean, simple picture without other buildings crowding the frame. Once you have the wide view, move closer and look for details: the Byzantine-style facade and the golden domes, which you can shoot from several angles along the front of the church.

For a different picture, the park behind the cathedral, Bērnu rotaļu laukums Park, shows the gold domes standing out in front of the trees.

Photography is prohibited inside the cathedral according to several pages, so plan to shoot only from outside. Keep your phone steady against your body, give the building a little space at the edges of the frame, and take a few shots at different zoom levels before moving on.
text.geographic_location: In central Riga, beside the Esplanade park, which is where the cathedral is best seen as a whole.
text.directions_text: Head for the Esplanade in central Riga. Walk east towards the domes if you want to go closer. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole cathedral across the park. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the golden domes and facade details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close and want to fit the full front in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Esplanade (the park in central Riga where the cathedral can be seen). The cathedral seen across the open green park space, with the building standing large and unobstructed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the cathedral on the upper third lines, with the lawn filling the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. For an alternative, try the park behind the cathedral (Bērnu rotaļu laukums Park), where the gold domes stand out in front of the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cathedral to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the gilded domes keep their detail against the sky. Take a Live Photo if people are walking through the park, so you can choose the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the gilded domes best, and the park is generally quieter early in the day.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship where photography is prohibited inside, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters gilded domes.
The park is generally quieter early in the day.
Reducing exposure slightly helps keep detail in bright gilded surfaces against the sky.
It takes about 2 minutes on foot from the stand-here point to the cathedral, based on straight-line distance.

name: St. James's Cathedral
label: St. James's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jēkaba iela' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jēkaba iela nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/171924063: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. James's Cathedral' (60 m across).
notes: Catholic cathedral with Latvia's oldest church tower.

text.description: St James's Cathedral is the Catholic cathedral of Riga, and its slim medieval spire is one of the easiest landmarks to pick out among the rooftops of the Old Town. The church was dedicated in 1225. It has changed hands several times, serving Lutherans, Jesuits and Catholics at different periods, and became the Catholic cathedral after 1923. Popes have visited twice, John Paul II in 1993 and Francis in 2018. It sits directly opposite the building where Latvia's parliament, the Saeima, meets, and that is what makes the picture so good. From the lane called Jēkaba iela you can fit the cobbles, the spire and the 19th-century parliament building into one frame. One guide even calls the cathedral's entrance the prettiest door in the Old Town, so it is worth a close-up. The interior is plain, so the outside is the main subject. Start with a wide shot along the lane, then move closer for the door and the stonework. Keep your phone upright and level, using the gridlines, so the spire does not lean. If the lane is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the passers-by. A short alternative is the view from Noliktavas iela, which gives a street-level look at the cathedral from a different direction.
text.geographic_location: In Old Riga (the Old Town), a UNESCO World Heritage Site, directly opposite the building where the Saeima, Latvia's parliament, meets.
text.directions_text: Make your way into the Old Town and head for St James's Cathedral (Svētā Jēkaba katedrāle). Then walk to Jēkaba iela, the lane beside the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the lane, spire and parliament building together, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the spire and the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jēkaba iela (looking along the lane toward the cathedral's spire, with the Saeima building alongside). The slim medieval spire rising above the cobbled lane, with the 19th-century parliament building beside it in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line a vertical edge up with one of them, so the buildings stay straight. Keep the cobbled lane in the lower part of the frame to lead the eye to the spire. For an alternative, try the view from the Noliktavas iela direction, but check it on the ground. Move closer afterwards for the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps some colour. Keep the flash off, as it is not allowed inside anyway and does nothing for a building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the lane. Photography is fine outside service hours, but do not walk around with your camera during Mass.

text.access_note: The outside is public street space, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting times and rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the Old Town lanes.
Tilting a phone upwards at a tall spire makes the vertical lines lean, so keeping the phone level helps.
The ultra-wide lens helps to fit the lane, spire and parliament building into one frame.

name: Large Guild
label: Great Guild
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Līvu laukums' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Līvu laukums' (way/45548895): middle (74 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/173411372: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Great Guild' (66 m across).
notes: Historic guild hall, now a concert hall.

text.description:
The Large Guild (Lielā ģilde, also called the Great Guild) is a Gothic-style building in Old Riga, on Amatu iela beside Līvu laukums. The current building dates from 1854–1859, in an English Gothic, Tudor-flavoured style. The guild itself goes back much further: its statute was recognised in 1353, and that year is counted as its founding. It is one of the oldest public buildings in the Baltic states and is the home hall of the Latvian National Symphony Orchestra.

It photographs well because the square in front of it is open and cobbled, so you can step back far enough to fit the pointed gables and tall windows into one frame. The Cat House stands at the same end of the square, and its rooftop cats can sit in the same picture, which gives the view a bit of fun as well as grandeur.

The building is under renovation, with work expected to finish by the end of 2026, so parts of the facade may be hidden or look different from older pictures. The interior is a concert hall, so check the official site before you go if you hope to go inside or photograph indoors.
text.geographic_location: In Old Riga (Vecrīga), on Amatu iela, facing Līvu laukums (Livonian Square) and close to the Cat House.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. Head for Old Riga and Līvu laukums on foot. From there the Large Guild is about 1 minute on foot, roughly 87 m to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the Cat House roof and the guild building together. Use 2x or more for the windows and gables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Līvu laukums (Cat House end of the square, looking across at the guild's facade). The Great Guild's Gothic facade across the open square, with the Cat House's rooftop cats in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight by holding the phone upright, not tilted back. Put the guild on one side of the frame and the Cat House roof on the other, with cobbles in the foreground for depth. Then step forward and use 2x or more for close details of the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. If a Live Photo is on, it can catch passers-by crossing the square; choose the sharpest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people on the square, and soft or overcast light shows the stonework evenly. Evening is also pleasant, but look at the facade before you shoot to check how the light falls.

text.access_note: The square is open public space, but the building is a concert hall under renovation, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Scaffolding or hoardings may cover parts of the facade while renovation continues.
Early morning on the square is usually quieter, with fewer people in the frame.
Soft or overcast light shows stonework evenly and avoids harsh shadows.
Holding the phone upright helps keep vertical lines straight on a tall facade.

name: St. Saviour's Church
label: St. Saviour's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St. Saviour's Church, Anglikanu iela 2a' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/171926518: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Anglikāņu baznīca' (44 m across).
notes: Small church beside the Dome Square old town.

text.description:
St. Saviour's Church is a neo-Gothic brick church with a slender bell tower, set just north of Riga's old town. It was designed by Johann Felsko. The foundation stone was laid in 1857 and the church was consecrated on 26 July 1859. It belongs to the Church of England and still has an active congregation. During the Soviet years it stopped being used for worship, and in 1973 it became a student club. Worship returned after Latvia regained independence in 1991.

It photographs well because the church sits slightly raised above the street, with a few trees and open ground in front. That gives you a clean, straight-on view of the facade and tower without much clutter. The forecourt is generally described as quiet and pleasant, so you can take your time over the shot.

Start with the whole facade and tower in one frame. Then move in for details such as the brickwork, the pointed windows and the top of the tower. Keep your phone upright so the tower has room to rise, and check the gridlines so the walls look straight rather than leaning. The trees can help as a natural frame at the edge of the picture. If the sky is bright, tap on the brickwork to set focus and lower the exposure slightly so the sky keeps some colour.
text.geographic_location: In Riga, just north of the old town centre (Vecrīga), close to Riga Castle and the banks of the Daugava River. The church is on Anglikāņu iela.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so head for the northern edge of the old town (Vecrīga) and walk towards Riga Castle and the Daugava. The church lies just north of the old town centre, close to the castle and the river. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the tower will not fit, but keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the top of the tower and the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is St. Saviour's Church itself, Anglikanu iela 2a. To take the shot, stand on the open ground in front of the street-facing facade. From there you see the neo-Gothic brick front and slender bell tower framed by the trees and open ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line. Let the trees frame one or both sides, and keep the church's slightly raised position in view so it feels set above the street. Take a wide shot first, then a closer telephoto shot of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. If people wander through the forecourt, a short burst or a Live Photo gives you a few frames to choose from.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters brick best. Check where the sun falls on the facade when you arrive.

text.access_note: The exterior can be photographed from the open space in front; it is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Latvian National Opera
label: National Opera
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fountain Nymph at Latvian National Opera House' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q555773: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Neoclassical opera house beside the Bastion Hill canal.

text.description:
The Latvian National Opera and Ballet stands at Aspazijas boulevard 3, on the bank of the Riga Canal and close to the Freedom Monument. The company has performed here since 1919. The building itself dates from 1860–1863, when it was put up as the Riga City Theatre. It burnt down in June 1882, leaving only the outer walls, and was rebuilt between 1882 and 1887 to a design by the city architect Reinhold Schmaeling. Inside, the Great Hall seats 946 people, and the season runs from mid-September to the end of May.

For a phone photo, the best spot is right in front of the opera, beside the ornate fountain. The sculpture makes a strong foreground and the building sits behind it, which gives the picture depth and a clear subject. If you have time, the park in front of the building also works. Bastejkalna Park gives you the facade framed by trees and lawns, and Kronvalda Park shows the opera across the canal with trees and reflections in the foreground.

Keep your shots to the outside of the building. Photography is not allowed during performances, so inside you could only photograph the curtain call. Stay clear of the pavement and entrance so you don't block people arriving for a show.
text.geographic_location: In central Riga, on Aspazijas boulevard beside the Riga Canal, a short walk from the Freedom Monument. The fountain stands right in front of the opera building.
text.directions_text: There is no tram or Underground-style stop right at this spot, so start from the Freedom Monument, which is close by, and follow the Riga Canal to the opera on Aspazijas boulevard. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Aspazijas bulvāris 3. The fountain is in front of the building, so you will see it as you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the fountain and the opera both sit comfortably in the frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are too close to fit the facade in. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the sculpture or the building's decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Position yourself in front of the building so the ornate fountain fills the foreground and the opera sits behind it in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fountain sculpture low in the frame with the opera behind it, and turn on gridlines to keep the building's lines straight. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning walls. For a different view, try Bastejkalna Park, where trees and lawns frame the facade, or Kronvalda Park, where the canal gives you reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out the building. If the water is moving, try a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the building and the fountain. After dark, try night mode, and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The fountain and the space in front of the opera are outdoors, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, and remember photography is not allowed during performances.
